newsitem.title: GERMANY: German shares go into Easter in cautious mood.
newsitem.headline: German shares go into Easter in cautious mood.

text.p: Caution dominated the German share market on Thursday as dealers braced themselves for an uncertain world picture when trading resumes here on Tuesday.
The IBIS DAX index was trailing down 8.76 at 3,430.46 at 1500 GMT, having tracked a zig zag course over the day.
"The share market will see stronger volatility in the coming weeks," Commerzbank warned in a note to investors.

"More favourable prospects for the German economy and the resultant opportunities for more improvements in corporate earnings will be offset by possible pressure from the foreign exchange and interest rate side."
Despite the long-anticipated U.S. rate hike, the DAX has risen four percent this week.
On the one hand, dealers said institutional investor interest was ensuring ample liquidity in the market, particularly for bank and car shares, which have been in vogue this week.
But at the same time, bearish talk that this week's U.S. interest rate hike was not the last was also circulating.
"A lot of the rise on Wednesday, for example, was due to short-covering, which makes me wonder how these high levels can be sustained," said a Frankfurt trader.
Car shares were the stars of the day, with the DAX 100 car sector index advancing six times faster than the market average, with a 1.8 percent overall gain.
In post-bourse IBIS trade, BMW AG was up 21 marks at 1,348 marks and Volkswagen AG was up 29 marks at 930 marks.
Lehman Brothers earlier upped its target price for BMW to 1,600 marks from 1,300.
However Daimler-Benz AG, which surged late on Wednesday after reporting a firm recovery in 1996, eased off its highs to trade down 2.20 marks at 133.60 marks.
Bank shares, which have surged this week amid fresh merger talk mostly fuelled by rumour, showed a varied performance.
Bayerische Vereinsbank AG was up two marks at 69.45 marks while Bayerische Hypotheken und Wechsel-Bank AG, Wednesday's strongest gainer, was down 16 pfennigs at 58.10 marks.

"Everyone wants into banks again all at once," commented one trader. "Although we've seen this week what we can expect from hostile takeover attempts in Germany," he added, referring to the aborted takeover bid by Krupp AG for steel firm Thyssen AG.
Thyssen was up 3.50 marks at 378 marks in afternoon trade, stabilising as details gradually emerged about its planned joint venture with Krupp, of which it will hold 60 percent.

The news has generally been viewed as a negative for the German financial markets, which had perked up at the chance of an Anglo-Saxon style takeover, but also revived talk of consolidation in the overcrowded banking industry.
